newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Bonds seen range bound on Weds.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Bonds seen range bound on Weds.

text.p: Bond prices likely would straddle current ranges on Wednesday as market participants awaited the critical nonfarm payrolls report on Friday.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics revised its seasonal adjustment factors last Friday, leaving many economists scrambling to revise their estimates on job creation in May downward -- some by as much as 100,000. Economists polled by Reuters had expected jobs to grow by 221,000 in the month. However, following the BLS adjustment they called for growth to come in at a slightly lesser rate of 219,000 on Tuesday.
"It's going to be quiet. The market is just responding to news" ahead of Friday's payrolls report, said John Mueller, senior vice president and chief economist at Lehrman Bell Mueller Cannon Inc.

"The economic data had been stronger, but now are weaker," Mueller said. He saw GDP growth slowing to a 2.0 percent rise in the second quarter following the robust 5.6 percent increase in the first quarter.
That would enable the Federal Reserve's policy-making FOMC to refrain from tightening monetary policy at its next meeting on July 1 and 2, Mueller said.

Maureen Mooney, senior analyst at GovPX, said volume at noon on Tuesday was about average, but bill volume was light compared to coupons. Analysts expected volume would remain contained before payrolls on Friday.
Brian Wesbury, economist at Griffen, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc, said that with long bond yields slipping below 6.90 percent, market psychology had shifted.
"We could see 6.75 percent in the next week and 6.50 percent before the end of the year," Wesbury said. "The huge buildup in inventories suggests we have to see a slowdown in production."
Real consumption in February, March and April rose only 0.2 percent, Wesbury said, leaving the Federal Reserve ample room to abstain from taking any action at its July meeting.
Wesbury expected nonfarm payrolls would have grown by 165,000 in May. The 34,000 average growth in retail jobs seen over the past three months suggested a slowdown in sales and consumption, he said.
"Flat retail sales in May would offset any gains in manufacturing," Wesbury said. "It doesn't matter what production does if the demand is not there."
The only data set for release on Wednesday were factory orders at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, but it was not expected to be a market-moving number, analysts said.
Given that, technical factors were likely to dominate trading flows throughout the session, economists said.

However, the market could get some support from a budget agreement. Senate Republicans said on Tuesday they were attempting to reach agreement with Democrats to give final approval this week to the fiscal 1998 budget. Economists said such an agreement would produce short-term gains.
